scenes.tts: After a meal, the sugar level in your blood rises. Small cells in your pancreas, called beta cells, then release insulin. Insulin is a protein hormone. The instructions for insulin are stored in the cell's nucleus. But the hormone leaves at the cell's outer edge. How does it get from one place to the other?
scenes.visual: Cell outline with a nucleus at left and the outer edge at right; a protein dot marked with question marks between them.
scenes.narration: After a meal, the sugar level in your blood rises. Small cells in your pancreas, called beta cells, then release insulin. Insulin is a protein hormone. The instructions for insulin are stored in the cell's nucleus. But the hormone leaves at the cell's outer edge. How does it get from one place to the other?

scenes.tts: Start in the nucleus. The nucleus holds most of the cell's D N A, its instructions. The gene for insulin is a stretch of D N A. The cell copies that gene into messenger R N A. Then the messenger R N A leaves the nucleus.
scenes.visual: Nucleus zooms in; DNA block, a copy as messenger RNA that leaves toward the ER.
scenes.caption: Start in the nucleus. The nucleus holds most of the cell's DNA, its instructions. The gene for insulin is a stretch of DNA. The cell copies that gene into messenger RNA. Then the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
scenes.narration: Start in the nucleus. The nucleus holds most of the cell's DNA, its instructions. The gene for insulin is a stretch of DNA. The cell copies that gene into messenger RNA. Then the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.

scenes.tts: The messenger R N A reaches a ribosome. A ribosome builds proteins. It reads the messenger R N A and links building blocks into a protein chain. The chain threads into the endoplasmic reticulum, or E R. Ribosomes dot the rough E R. There, the new protein folds. In a beta cell, this chain is a longer precursor, cut into insulin later.
scenes.visual: Ribosome dots on the rough ER; protein appears and passes into the ER.
scenes.caption: The messenger RNA reaches a ribosome. A ribosome builds proteins. It reads the messenger RNA and links building blocks into a protein chain. The chain threads into the endoplasmic reticulum, or ER. Ribosomes dot the rough ER. There, the new protein folds. In a beta cell, this chain is a longer precursor, cut into insulin later.
scenes.narration: The messenger RNA reaches a ribosome. A ribosome builds proteins. It reads the messenger RNA and links building blocks into a protein chain. The chain threads into the endoplasmic reticulum, or ER. Ribosomes dot the rough ER. There, the new protein folds. In a beta cell, this chain is a longer precursor, cut into insulin later.

scenes.tts: Next, a vesicle forms. A vesicle is a small bubble of membrane that carries materials. It buds off the E R and delivers the protein to the Golgi apparatus. The Golgi sorts the protein and packs it into new vesicles. Insulin is stored in these vesicles until it is needed.
scenes.visual: Vesicle buds from ER, travels to Golgi; new vesicles bud from Golgi and wait.
scenes.caption: Next, a vesicle forms. A vesicle is a small bubble of membrane that carries materials. It buds off the ER and delivers the protein to the Golgi apparatus. The Golgi sorts the protein and packs it into new vesicles. Insulin is stored in these vesicles until it is needed.

scenes.tts: When blood sugar rises, more of these vesicles fuse with the cell membrane. Each vesicle then releases insulin outside the cell. Beta cells also release a smaller amount between meals. Building a protein chain and moving vesicles both use energy. Mitochondria release energy from sugar and store it in A T P. A T P carries energy in a form cell parts can use.
scenes.visual: Vesicles fuse with the outer edge and release insulin; mitochondria with ATP arrows to the steps.

Beta cells also release a smaller amount between meals. Building a protein chain and moving vesicles both use energy. Mitochondria release energy from sugar and store it in ATP. ATP carries energy in a form cell parts can use.
scenes.narration: When blood sugar rises, more of these vesicles fuse with the cell membrane. Each vesicle then releases insulin outside the cell. Beta cells also release a smaller amount between meals. Building a protein chain and moving vesicles both use energy. Mitochondria release energy from sugar and store it in ATP. scenes.tts: So how do the parts of a cell work together? Each part hands its product to the next. The nucleus keeps the instructions. Ribosomes build the protein, and the E R folds it. Vesicles carry it, and the Golgi sorts and packs it. The membrane lets it out. Mitochondria supply the A T P along the way. A factory is a useful model, but no manager gives orders.
scenes.visual: Whole route lit part by part in order with mitochondria ATP; final line about the model.
